_comment: Authored, topic-tagged curriculum questions used by module checkpoints. Unlike the upload-to-quiz flow these are not model generated, so topic mastery is measured against stable, reviewed items.

T01.stem: A household survey draws its sample from a list of dwellings compiled three years ago. Newly constructed colonies are absent from that list. What error does this introduce?
options: Sampling error that shrinks as n grows
Processing error at the tabulation stage
T01.explanation: Units that exist in the population but are missing from the frame are under-covered. This is a frame defect, not a sampling or processing problem.

T01.stem: Why can post-survey weighting NOT repair coverage error in the sampling frame?
options: Coverage error affects only the variance, never the point estimate
Weights must sum to the sample size, not the population
Units missing from the frame had no chance of selection, so no respondent represents them
Weighting is only valid for stratified designs
T01.explanation: Weighting redistributes the responses you did obtain. A unit with zero selection probability is represented by nobody, so no weight can stand in for it.

T01.stem: A frame lists some commercial premises twice under slightly different names. If this is not detected, the estimates will be affected by:
options: Over-coverage, giving those units an inflated chance of selection
A reduction in the design effect
T01.explanation: Duplicate frame entries are over-coverage: the duplicated unit has roughly twice the selection probability it should have.

T01.stem: For rural household surveys in India, the sampling frame at the first stage is most commonly built from:
options: The electoral roll of the district
T01.explanation: Census village lists provide the standard first-stage frame in rural areas; urban areas use Census enumeration blocks.

T02.stem: Stratification reduces the variance of an estimator most when strata are:
options: Internally homogeneous and different from each other on the study variable
Equal in size regardless of their composition
Internally varied so each contains the full range of values
Formed at random from the frame
T02.explanation: The gain comes from removing between-stratum variation from the sampling error. Homogeneous strata that differ from one another maximise that gain.

T02.stem: Under proportional allocation, the number of units sampled from a stratum is set in proportion to:
options: The size of the stratum in the population
The response rate achieved in the previous round
The variance of the study variable in the stratum
The cost of enumerating one unit in the stratum
T02.explanation: Proportional allocation uses stratum size alone. Optimal (Neyman) allocation is what brings variance and cost into the calculation.

T02.stem: Optimal allocation assigns a LARGER sample to a stratum when that stratum has:
options: Low variability and high cost per unit
High variability in the study variable and low cost per unit
T02.explanation: Neyman allocation puts effort where variance is high and enumeration is cheap; both push the allocated sample up.

T02.stem: An officer stratifies an establishment survey by employment size band. This is sensible mainly because:
options: Turnover and employment are strongly related, so size bands are homogeneous on the study variable
Size bands always contain equal numbers of establishments
It removes the need for weighting
It guarantees a higher response rate
T02.explanation: A good stratifier correlates with the study variable. Establishment size does, which is why size-band stratification is near-universal.

T03.stem: The design weight of a sampled unit is:
options: The number of units in its stratum
The reciprocal of its probability of selection
The ratio of the sample size to the population size
T03.explanation: A unit selected with probability 1/500 represents about 500 units, so its design weight is 500.

T03.stem: In a two-stage design, villages are selected with probability proportional to population and a fixed number of households is taken in each. The effect on household selection probabilities is that they are:
options: Undefined without a listing of all households
Approximately equal across villages, making the design self-weighting
T03.explanation: PPS at stage one and a fixed take at stage two offset each other, producing roughly equal overall probabilities. This is the classic self-weighting design.

T03.stem: Calibration adjusts survey weights so that:
options: Weighted survey totals match known population benchmarks
The sample size matches the target
Imputed values equal the observed mean
Every respondent carries the same weight
T03.explanation: Calibration forces agreement with external totals such as projected population by age and sex, reducing bias and often variance.

T03.stem: Treating a multi-stage stratified sample as if it were a simple random sample when estimating variance will typically:
T03.explanation: Clustering makes observations within a PSU positively correlated. Ignoring it understates variance, sometimes badly.

T04.stem: An edit rule flags a record where a respondent's age is 12 and marital status is 'widowed'. This is best described as:
options: A consistency edit between two related fields
A range edit on a single field
T04.explanation: Range edits check one field against permitted values; consistency edits check the relationship between fields, as here.

T04.stem: The purpose of selective editing is to:
options: Remove all records that fail any edit rule
Concentrate limited review effort on records whose correction would most change the published aggregate
Edit every record to the same standard
Replace failed records with imputed values automatically
T04.explanation: Selective editing scores records by their likely influence on the estimate, so scarce analyst time goes where it changes the published figure.

T04.stem: A large establishment reports turnover 40 times its previous return. Before treating this as an outlier, the analyst should FIRST:
options: Check whether a genuine change such as a merger or unit-of-measure error explains it
Delete the record from the dataset
Replace the value with the industry mean
Reduce the weight of the record to zero
T04.explanation: Extreme values are often real or a simple unit error (rupees versus lakh). Investigate before altering, since large units carry heavy weight.

T04.stem: Over-editing is a risk because it:
options: Consumes resources and can introduce bias by smoothing genuine variation
Reduces the sample size below the design target
T04.explanation: Editing everything costs time and can quietly pull true extreme values toward the middle, biasing dispersion measures.

T05.stem: Data are 'missing completely at random' (MCAR) when the probability of a value being missing:
options: Does not depend on observed or unobserved data
Depends on the missing value itself
Is the same in every stratum by design
T05.explanation: MCAR is the strongest and rarest assumption. MAR depends on observed data; MNAR depends on the unobserved value itself.

T05.stem: Compared with mean imputation, hot-deck donor imputation is generally preferred because it:
options: Preserves the distribution of the variable rather than piling values at the mean
Removes the need to record which values were imputed
T05.explanation: Mean imputation artificially shrinks variance. Donor methods take a real value from a similar responding unit, keeping the shape of the distribution.

T05.stem: Why must imputed values be flagged in the microdata?
options: It allows imputed records to be deleted before publication
Flagging is required before weighting can be applied
Imputation adds uncertainty that naive variance estimates ignore
T05.explanation: Treating imputed values as if they were observed understates variance. The flag lets users apply methods that account for imputation uncertainty.

T05.stem: Item non-response differs from unit non-response in that item non-response is:
options: A missing answer to some questions from a responding unit
A refusal by the entire household to participate
A unit missing from the sampling frame
T05.explanation: Unit non-response means the whole unit is lost and is handled by weighting; item non-response is handled by imputation.

options: Does not necessarily shrink as the sample size grows
Can be estimated directly from the sample variance
Is removed by increasing the number of strata
T06.explanation: Doubling the sample can double the volume of measurement and processing error. Only sampling error is guaranteed to fall with n.

T06.stem: In large official surveys, non-sampling error compared with sampling error is:
T06.explanation: At large sample sizes sampling error is small, which leaves measurement, processing and non-response as the dominant error sources.

T06.stem: Independent re-interview of a subsample is used primarily to:
T06.explanation: Re-interview compares an independent measurement against the original to quantify measurement and interviewer variance.

T06.stem: A quality report accompanying a statistical release would normally include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Coefficients of variation for key estimates
T06.explanation: Respondent identity is protected by statistical confidentiality. Response, imputation and precision measures are standard quality indicators.

T07.stem: Which question is double-barrelled and should be split?
options: In the last 30 days, did you seek medical treatment?
Are you satisfied with the quality and the timeliness of the release?
How many persons usually reside in this household?
T07.explanation: It asks about two attributes at once. A respondent satisfied with quality but not timeliness cannot answer accurately.

T07.stem: A closed question with pre-coded options is preferred over an open question mainly when:
options: The full range of plausible answers is known in advance
T07.explanation: Pre-coding is only safe when the option list is exhaustive. If it is not, open capture with later coding avoids forcing wrong answers.

T07.stem: Lengthening the recall period in a consumption survey from 7 days to 30 days typically:
options: Improves accuracy for all item types equally
Has no effect on reported expenditure
Reduces recall accuracy for small frequent purchases
T07.explanation: Longer reference periods lose small, frequent items to forgetting; short periods suit frequent purchases and long periods suit rare large ones.

T07.stem: A response scale offering 'Excellent, Good, Good, Poor' is defective because the options are not:
T07.explanation: Duplicated categories mean the same answer maps to two codes, so responses cannot be interpreted.

T08.stem: Sensitive questions are usually placed late in an interview because:
options: The respondent has invested time and rapport has been built
T08.explanation: Asking sensitive items early risks a break-off that costs the whole interview. Late placement means earlier answers are already secured.

T08.stem: A skip pattern instructs the interviewer to:
options: Omit every third question to save time
Bypass questions that do not apply given an earlier answer
Return to a previous section for verification
T08.explanation: Filters route the respondent past inapplicable blocks, for instance skipping employment detail for a respondent not in the labour force.

T08.stem: Opening a household questionnaire with straightforward demographic items rather than income questions is intended to:
options: Establish rapport and reduce early break-off
T08.explanation: Easy, non-threatening openers build cooperation before harder material arrives.

T08.stem: In a paper instrument, a complex nest of skip instructions is risky chiefly because:
options: Interviewers may misroute, creating missing or invalid data
T08.explanation: Manual routing errors are a well documented source of item non-response on paper; CAPI enforces routing automatically.

T09.stem: The main data-quality advantage of CAPI over a paper schedule is that CAPI:
options: Enforces skip patterns and range checks at the moment of collection
Removes the need for a sampling frame
T09.explanation: Validating at the doorstep prevents errors that would otherwise be found weeks later in editing, when the respondent is unreachable.

T09.stem: A CAPI hard check should be reserved for values that are:
options: Logically impossible, since it blocks the interviewer from proceeding
T09.explanation: Hard checks on merely unusual values force interviewers to enter false data to move on. Soft warnings suit implausible-but-possible values.

T09.stem: CATI is generally less suitable than CAPI for rural household surveys in India mainly because of:
options: Uneven telephone coverage, which biases who can be reached
The absence of skip logic in CATI systems
T09.explanation: Telephone frames under-cover exactly the households of most interest, introducing coverage bias that weighting cannot fully repair.

T09.stem: Paradata such as interview timestamps and question timings are useful mainly for:
options: Detecting interviewer falsification and problem questions
T09.explanation: Implausibly fast interviews or a question that consistently takes very long are signals for supervision and instrument revision.

T10.stem: Household income in a district is strongly right-skewed by a few very high earners. The better measure of a typical household is the:
T10.explanation: The mean is pulled toward the long right tail. The median is unaffected by how extreme the extremes are.

T10.stem: The coefficient of variation is useful because it:
options: Expresses dispersion relative to the mean, allowing comparison across different units
Is always smaller than the standard deviation
Converts any distribution to a normal one
T10.explanation: As a ratio it is unitless, so the variability of turnover in rupees can be compared with the variability of employment in persons.

T10.stem: In a cross-tabulation of employment status by education level, the cell percentages should be computed on the row total when the question of interest is:
options: How employment status differs across education levels
How many people are in each cell
The sampling error of the table
T10.explanation: Percentaging within the explanatory category (education) lets you compare the outcome distribution across those categories.

T10.stem: A distribution with a long left tail is described as:
T10.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the tail; a long left tail means negative skew, with mean typically below median.

T11.stem: The standard error of a sample mean measures:
options: The spread of individual values in the population
How much the sample mean would vary across repeated samples
The largest error made by any interviewer
T11.explanation: The standard deviation describes individuals; the standard error describes the sampling distribution of the estimate itself.

T11.stem: To halve the standard error of a mean under simple random sampling, the sample size must be multiplied by approximately:
T11.explanation: The standard error falls with the square root of n, so a fourfold increase in sample size halves it. Precision is expensive.

T11.stem: A 95% confidence interval for mean household size is 4.1 to 4.5. The correct interpretation is that:
options: Under repeated sampling, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean
There is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this particular interval
95% of households have between 4.1 and 4.5 members
The sample mean has a 5% chance of being wrong
T11.explanation: The confidence level is a property of the procedure across repetitions, not a probability statement about one fixed interval.

T11.stem: The design effect of a survey compares its variance with that of:
options: A simple random sample of the same size
The previous round of the same survey
A stratified sample of twice the size
T11.explanation: Deff above 1 means clustering has cost precision relative to SRS; it is the standard summary of a complex design's efficiency.

options: If the null hypothesis were true, data this extreme would occur 3% of the time
There is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true
The result will replicate 97% of the time
T12.explanation: The p-value is computed assuming the null is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and says nothing about replication.

T12.stem: A Type I error occurs when an analyst:
options: Rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true
Fails to reject a null hypothesis that is false
T12.explanation: Type I is a false positive, controlled by the significance level. Type II is a false negative, controlled by power and sample size.

T12.stem: With a very large sample, a statistically significant difference may still be unimportant because:
options: Large samples always violate the assumptions of the test
Significance testing detects tiny effects that carry no practical meaning
p-values cannot be computed for large samples
T12.explanation: Significance answers 'is there an effect', not 'is it big enough to matter'. Always report the effect size alongside the p-value.

T12.stem: Increasing the sample size in a hypothesis test primarily increases:
options: The probability of a Type I error
The power to detect a real effect
T12.explanation: Power is the chance of rejecting a false null. The significance level is chosen by the analyst, not driven by n.

T13.stem: In R, a column of district names read from a CSV is stored as a factor. Applying as.numeric() directly to it returns:
options: The integer codes of the factor levels, not the original values
An error that halts the script
T13.explanation: Factors are integers with labels. The safe idiom is as.numeric(as.character(x)); the direct conversion silently returns level codes.

T13.stem: A data frame differs from a matrix in R in that a data frame:
options: Can hold different types in different columns
Cannot be indexed by column name
T13.explanation: A matrix is a single type throughout; a data frame is a list of equal-length vectors that may each have their own type.

T13.stem: A survey file codes 'not applicable' as 99. If read without instruction, R will:
options: Treat 99 as a valid numeric value and include it in means
T13.explanation: Sentinel codes must be declared with na.strings or recoded, otherwise they silently contaminate every summary statistic.

T13.stem: When reading a fixed-width file, the essential extra information required is:
T13.explanation: Fixed-width files carry no delimiters, so the layout of start and end positions must be supplied from the record specification.

T14.stem: To produce mean expenditure by district from a household data frame, the appropriate operation is:
options: Group by district, then summarise the mean
Filter to one district at a time and bind the rows
Reshape to wide format, then average the columns
Sort by district, then take the overall mean
T14.explanation: Group-then-summarise is the standard split-apply-combine idiom and returns one row per district.

T14.stem: Data in 'long' format store one observation per:
options: Unit-and-variable combination, in a single value column
T14.explanation: Long format stacks measurements with a key column naming the variable; wide format spreads them across separate columns.

T14.stem: A left join of households to a district lookup table produces more rows than the household table had. The most likely cause is:
options: A missing value in the household table
The lookup table being sorted differently
Duplicate district keys in the lookup table
Using left instead of inner join
T14.explanation: A left join preserves every left row and multiplies against duplicate matches on the right. Deduplicate the lookup before joining.

T14.stem: Computing a mean in R when the vector contains NA returns NA unless you:
options: Pass na.rm = TRUE, having first decided that dropping them is appropriate
Convert the vector to a factor
T14.explanation: na.rm silences the NA but is a substantive decision: dropping missing values assumes they are missing at random.

T15.stem: A weighted mean should be used instead of an unweighted mean whenever:
options: Units were selected with unequal probabilities
T15.explanation: Unequal selection probabilities mean the sample does not mirror the population. Weights restore representativeness.

T15.stem: Applying design weights to point estimates but computing standard errors as if the sample were simple random will:
options: Give correct estimates with understated standard errors
Give incorrect estimates with correct standard errors
Produce an error in most software
T15.explanation: This is the most common analysis mistake with complex survey data: the estimate is fine, the stated precision is optimistic.

T15.stem: The main reason to write analysis as a script rather than clicking through a GUI is that a script:
options: Can be re-run to reproduce the exact published figures
T15.explanation: Reproducibility is the point: when a figure is queried months later, the script regenerates it exactly.

T15.stem: Setting a random seed before an imputation or a bootstrap ensures that:
options: The same results are obtained on every re-run
T15.explanation: A seed fixes the pseudo-random stream. It buys reproducibility only; it makes nothing statistically more valid.

T16.stem: The National Industrial Classification classifies a unit according to its:
T16.explanation: NIC classifies what the unit produces. NCO classifies what individual workers do.

T16.stem: The correct hierarchy of the NIC, from broadest to narrowest, is:
T16.explanation: Sections carry alphabetic codes; divisions, groups and classes progressively add digits to the numeric code.

T16.stem: An establishment both mills flour and runs a small retail counter. Under NIC it should be classified by:
options: The activity accounting for the greatest value added
The activity listed first in its registration
The retail activity, since it faces the customer
T16.explanation: The principal activity rule uses the largest share of value added, with employment or turnover as practical proxies.

T16.stem: A unit that assembles garments entirely from material owned by another firm, for a fee, is classified under:
options: Manufacturing, because the transformation activity determines the class
T16.explanation: Physical transformation places the unit in manufacturing regardless of who owns the inputs; this contract-work case is a classic coding trap.

T17.stem: The National Classification of Occupations classifies:
options: The kind of work a person performs
The industry of the employing unit
The wage band of the worker
T17.explanation: NCO describes the job itself. Two people in the same industry can hold very different occupations.

T17.stem: In the NCO, the concept of 'skill level' broadly corresponds to:
options: The size of the employing establishment
The number of years the person has worked
The complexity and range of tasks in the job
T17.explanation: Skill level reflects task complexity, usually associated with a level of education or training, not tenure or pay.

T17.stem: An accountant employed by a textile mill is coded in NIC and NCO respectively as:
T17.explanation: NIC follows the employer's activity, NCO follows the worker's job. Conflating the two is the most frequent classification error.

T17.stem: 'Skill specialisation' in the NCO refers to the:
options: Field of knowledge, tools and materials the job involves
T17.explanation: Skill level sets the broad major group; skill specialisation distinguishes occupations within that level.

T18.stem: A field return records activity as 'shop'. The correct action by the coder is to:
options: Refer it back for more detail, since the description is too vague to code
Assign the most common retail code
Code it as manufacturing by default
T18.explanation: Guessing propagates an error into the published aggregate. Insufficient descriptions should be queried, not resolved by assumption.

T18.stem: The most common cause of misclassification between NIC and NCO in field returns is:
options: Recording the employer's industry in the occupation field
Use of the previous year's classification version
Coding at too detailed a level
T18.explanation: Enumerators frequently write 'railways' or 'hospital' as the occupation. The occupation field needs the job, not the workplace.

T18.stem: Independent double-coding of a subsample of returns is used to:
options: Replace the need for a coding manual
T18.explanation: Two coders working independently on the same descriptions give a direct measure of coding reliability.

T18.stem: When a classification is revised between survey rounds, comparability over time is preserved by:
options: Publishing a concordance between old and new codes
Coding everything to the old version indefinitely
Aggregating to the section level only
T18.explanation: A concordance maps old codes to new so series can be bridged; back-casting key aggregates usually accompanies it.

T19.stem: Under the SNA production boundary, which activity is EXCLUDED from GDP?
options: Unpaid domestic housework performed for one's own household
T19.explanation: Own-account production of goods counts, and imputed housing rent counts, but unpaid household services such as cooking and cleaning for one's own household sit outside the boundary.

T19.stem: The imputed rent of owner-occupied dwellings is included in GDP in order to:
options: Keep GDP comparable between economies where renting is more or less common
T19.explanation: Without the imputation, an economy where households own their homes would appear to produce less housing service than an otherwise identical renting economy.

T19.stem: Which institutional sector do government-owned enterprises selling at economically significant prices belong to?
T19.explanation: Sector is decided by economic behaviour, not ownership: a market producer is a corporation even when the State owns it.

T19.stem: Intermediate consumption refers to goods and services that are:
options: Used up in the production process during the accounting period
Held as fixed assets over several years
T19.explanation: Intermediate consumption is fully consumed within the period; durable items used repeatedly are fixed capital instead.

T20.stem: Gross value added is calculated as:
T20.explanation: GVA measures the value a producer adds beyond the inputs it consumes.

T20.stem: To move from GVA at basic prices to GDP at market prices you:
options: Add taxes on products and subtract subsidies on products
T20.explanation: Basic prices exclude product taxes and include product subsidies, so the adjustment reverses both.

T20.stem: Constant-price GVA is used rather than current-price GVA when the aim is to measure:
options: Real growth in output, free of price change
The current size of the economy in rupees
The share of wages in output
T20.explanation: Deflating to constant prices strips out inflation so that changes reflect volume rather than price.

T20.stem: Double deflation compiles real GVA by deflating:
options: Only output, using the GDP deflator
Value added directly with the CPI
Output and intermediate consumption separately with their own price indices
T20.explanation: Because input and output prices can move differently, deflating each separately gives a more accurate volume measure than deflating GVA as a whole.

T21.stem: In the expenditure approach, GDP equals:
options: Wages plus profits plus rent plus interest
Consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports
T21.explanation: C + I + G + (X - M) sums final expenditures; imports are subtracted because they are not domestic production.

T21.stem: Imports are subtracted in the expenditure approach because they:
options: Are recorded at cost, insurance and freight values
Are already included in consumption and investment but were not domestically produced
T21.explanation: Spending totals include purchases of foreign goods, so the import deduction removes what the domestic economy did not produce.

T21.stem: The income approach measures GDP by summing:
options: Compensation of employees, gross operating surplus, mixed income and net production taxes
T21.explanation: It totals the incomes generated by production, which in principle equals the value of what was produced.

T21.stem: When the production, expenditure and income estimates of GDP differ, the difference is:
options: Always attributed to the informal sector
Evidence that one approach is theoretically wrong
A statistical discrepancy arising from independent data sources
T21.explanation: The three are equal by definition but measured from different sources, so a residual discrepancy is expected and reported.

T22.stem: A Laspeyres price index holds quantities fixed at:
T22.explanation: Laspeyres asks what the base-period basket costs now; Paasche uses current-period quantities instead.

T22.stem: The Laspeyres index tends to overstate the cost of living because it ignores:
options: Substitution away from goods whose relative prices have risen
T22.explanation: Consumers shift toward cheaper alternatives, but the fixed base basket assumes they do not, giving upward substitution bias.

T22.stem: A Fisher index is constructed as:
options: The arithmetic mean of the two
The geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices
The Laspeyres index divided by the Paasche index
T22.explanation: The geometric mean gives a superlative index that sits between the two and satisfies the time reversal test.

T22.stem: Chain drift occurs when an index that is chained frequently:
options: Fails to return to its original level after prices return to their starting values
Cannot be computed for missing items
Rises faster than the base-weighted index by definition
T22.explanation: With volatile prices and strong substitution, chaining can accumulate a bias so the index does not return to where it began.

T23.stem: CPI weights are normally derived from:
T23.explanation: Weights reflect how households actually allocate spending, which is measured by a consumption expenditure survey.

T23.stem: The main reason to revise the base year of a price index periodically is that:
options: Consumption patterns drift, so old weights stop representing current spending
The arithmetic becomes harder over time
T23.explanation: An outdated basket gives increasing weight to goods households no longer buy in the same proportion.

T23.stem: When a series is rebased, historical values are made comparable by:
options: Recomputing the old series with new weights
Linking the old and new series with an overlap factor
T23.explanation: A linking factor computed over an overlap period splices the series so the level is continuous.

T23.stem: A weighting diagram in a price index specifies:
options: The relative importance of each item group in total expenditure
The number of price quotations collected
T23.explanation: It is the structure of expenditure shares that determines how much each item influences the headline index.

T24.stem: When a specified item is permanently unavailable in an outlet, the correct action is to:
options: Drop the item from the index permanently
Select a comparable replacement and adjust for any quality difference
Carry the last observed price forward indefinitely
T24.explanation: Replacement keeps the sample representative, but the quality difference must be adjusted so a genuine price change is not confused with a specification change.

T24.stem: Failing to adjust for quality improvement when an item is replaced will typically:
T24.explanation: A better product at a higher price is partly paying for more quality; treating the whole rise as inflation overstates it.

T24.stem: Seasonal items that disappear for part of the year are commonly handled by:
options: Using the previous year's price unchanged
Imputing their price movement from similar available items
Setting their weight to zero permanently
T24.explanation: Imputation from a similar group keeps the index continuous without inventing a price observation.

T24.stem: Price collectors are instructed to record the price actually charged, including temporary discounts, because the index measures:
options: The list price set by manufacturers
T24.explanation: A consumer price index tracks transaction prices faced by households, so genuine discounts available to all buyers are in scope.

T25.explanation: Seventeen goals break into targets, and each target is monitored by one or more indicators.

T25.stem: India's National Indicator Framework differs from the global framework in that it:
options: Is compiled by the United Nations
Replaces the global goals with different ones
Selects and adapts indicators to national priorities and data availability
T25.explanation: National frameworks localise monitoring while remaining mapped to the global targets.

T25.stem: Which ministry is responsible for compiling India's National Indicator Framework?
options: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
T25.explanation: MoSPI compiles and publishes the NIF and its progress reports, working with line ministries that own the source data.

T25.stem: An indicator is best described as:
options: A measurable quantity that tracks progress toward a target
T25.explanation: Targets state the intent; indicators are the measurable evidence of movement toward it.

T26.stem: A Tier I SDG indicator is one that has:
options: An agreed methodology but little country data
An agreed methodology and data regularly produced by countries
T26.explanation: Tier II has methodology but sparse data; Tier III lacked an established methodology and the tier has since been phased out.

T26.stem: Administrative sources are often preferred to surveys for SDG reporting when:
options: The indicator requires attitudes or opinions
The programme itself records complete data on every beneficiary
T26.explanation: Registers can give complete counts cheaply and frequently, though their coverage and definitions must match the indicator.

T26.stem: A proxy indicator is used when:
options: Funding for surveys is unavailable this year
The concept cannot be measured directly with available data
The target has already been met
The true indicator is politically sensitive
T26.explanation: A proxy stands in for a concept that is hard to observe, and its limitations must be documented alongside it.

T26.stem: Combining data from several ministries for one indicator most often creates problems of:
options: Differing definitions, reference periods and coverage
T26.explanation: Harmonising concepts across sources is usually harder than the arithmetic of combining them.

T27.stem: Disaggregation of SDG indicators is required primarily to:
options: Increase the number of published tables
Reveal whether progress is leaving particular groups behind
T27.explanation: A national average can improve while a disadvantaged group stagnates; disaggregation by sex, location and social group exposes that.

T27.stem: A national average that improves while the gap between richest and poorest widens illustrates why:
options: Aggregate progress alone is an insufficient measure
T27.explanation: This is exactly the failure mode the leave-no-one-behind principle is designed to detect.

T27.stem: When disaggregating a survey-based indicator by district, the main statistical risk is:
options: Small sample sizes making estimates unreliable
T27.explanation: Surveys designed for state-level precision often cannot support district estimates without small-area estimation methods.

T27.stem: Estimates too imprecise to publish should be:
options: Suppressed or flagged with their reliability clearly stated
T27.explanation: Standard practice is to suppress or footnote estimates below a reliability threshold rather than let users treat them as firm.

T28.stem: To compare a single value across about twenty districts, the clearest chart is usually a:
options: Horizontal bar chart sorted by value
T28.explanation: Sorted bars let the reader rank and compare lengths precisely; pie slices and areas are much harder to compare.

T28.stem: Pie charts become unreliable mainly when:
options: There are many categories of similar size
T28.explanation: People judge angles poorly, so similar slices are indistinguishable; a bar chart shows the same data far more precisely.

T28.stem: A line chart is the right form when the horizontal axis represents:
options: A continuous ordered dimension such as time
T28.explanation: Connecting points implies continuity between them, which only makes sense for an ordered dimension.

T28.stem: To show the relationship between two continuous variables across units, use a:
T28.explanation: A scatter plot maps each unit to a point in two dimensions, revealing correlation, clusters and outliers.

T29.stem: In a published statistical table, figures should be rounded so that:
options: All columns have the same width
As many digits as possible are displayed
The precision shown matches the precision the data actually support
T29.explanation: Printing digits beyond what the estimate can support implies false accuracy to the reader.

T29.stem: When rounded components of a table do not sum to the rounded total, the correct response is to:
options: Add a footnote explaining that components may not sum due to rounding
Adjust one component so the total matches
Round everything to the nearest thousand
T29.explanation: Silently forcing components to add up misrepresents the underlying figures; a footnote is the standard convention.

T29.stem: Colour alone should not be used to convey meaning in a chart because:
options: Readers with colour vision deficiency may not distinguish the categories
T29.explanation: Accessible design pairs colour with a second channel such as position, pattern or a direct label.

T29.stem: Every published table should carry a unit statement because:
options: A number without its unit cannot be interpreted
It fills space in the header
T29.explanation: Rupees, lakh, thousands and percentages all look alike as bare digits; the unit is part of the datum.

T30.stem: Truncating the vertical axis of a bar chart so it does not start at zero:
options: Exaggerates the apparent difference between bars
Is required when values are large
T30.explanation: Bar length encodes magnitude, so a non-zero baseline distorts the very comparison the bars are meant to support.

T30.stem: Error bars on an estimate are included in order to show:
options: The range of the raw data
T30.explanation: They communicate that the point estimate is one draw from a distribution, not an exact value.

T30.stem: When two estimates have overlapping confidence intervals, it is safest to describe the difference as:
options: Not clearly distinguishable given the precision of the data
T30.explanation: Overlap does not prove equality, but it does mean the data cannot firmly separate the two.

T30.stem: An estimate with a very high coefficient of variation should be:
T30.explanation: Statistical offices set CV thresholds above which an estimate is footnoted or withheld to prevent misuse.

T31.stem: The Collection of Statistics Act primarily empowers the government to:
options: Collect statistical information and obliges respondents to furnish it
T31.explanation: The Act creates the legal basis for statistical collection and the corresponding duty on respondents to reply.

T31.stem: Information collected under the Act may be used for:
T31.explanation: The statistical-purpose restriction is what makes the guarantee of confidentiality credible to respondents.

T31.stem: A statistics officer who discloses an identifiable individual return to a colleague outside the statistical function has:
options: Acted properly if the data were anonymised afterwards
Breached the confidentiality provisions of the Act
Acted properly if the colleague is a government servant
Committed no offence if no harm resulted
T31.explanation: Access is restricted to those performing the statistical function, regardless of the recipient's employer or intentions.

T31.stem: The duty to furnish information under the Act falls on:
options: The respondent from whom the information is sought
T31.explanation: The Act places the obligation on the informant, with penalties for wilful refusal or knowingly false returns.

T32.stem: The confidentiality pledge given to respondents means their individual returns will:
options: Never be published or disclosed in identifiable form
Be shared only with their state government
Be available on request under transparency rules
T32.explanation: Only aggregates are released; the individual return is protected indefinitely.

T32.stem: A request under a transparency or right-to-information provision for individual survey returns should be:
options: Refused, because statistical confidentiality is a statutory exemption
Referred to the respondent for consent
T32.explanation: Statistical confidentiality is a recognised exemption; removing names alone rarely prevents re-identification.

T32.stem: Confidentiality obligations of a statistics officer end when:
options: They do not end, and continue after the officer leaves service
T32.explanation: The duty attaches to the information, not to the officer's current posting, and persists after they move on.

T32.stem: Sharing microdata with a university researcher is acceptable only when:
options: The data have been anonymised and released under a controlled access arrangement
The researcher signs no agreement but promises discretion
T32.explanation: Access regimes combine anonymisation, a legal agreement and often a secure environment, rather than relying on trust.

T33.stem: Indirect identification occurs when a person is recognised from:
options: A combination of attributes such as age, occupation and village
T33.explanation: Removing names is not enough: a rare combination of quasi-identifiers can single out one individual.

T33.stem: Cell suppression in a published table is applied when a cell:
options: Is based on too few units, risking identification
T33.explanation: Small counts can expose an individual, so cells below a threshold are suppressed.

options: A single suppressed cell can be recovered by subtraction from published totals
T33.explanation: Additional cells must be suppressed so the primary suppression cannot be reconstructed arithmetically from row and column totals.

T33.stem: k-anonymity requires that every combination of quasi-identifiers in a released file:
options: Appears for at least k individuals
T33.explanation: With at least k matching records, no single individual can be picked out from that combination alone.

T34.stem: An administrative register differs from a survey in that it is:
options: A by-product of running a programme, not designed for statistics
T34.explanation: Registers are built to administer a scheme, so their definitions and coverage follow programme rules rather than statistical need.

T34.stem: The most common problem when using a benefit register to measure poverty is that it covers:
options: Only those who applied and qualified, not everyone in need
T34.explanation: Eligibility and take-up filter the register, so it measures programme participation rather than the underlying condition.

T34.stem: Linking an administrative register to a survey frame requires:
options: A common identifier or reliable matching variables
T34.explanation: Without a shared key, probabilistic matching on name, age and address introduces both false matches and missed links.

T34.stem: A definitional mismatch arises when the register records:
options: Data in a different file format
A concept close to but not the same as the statistical concept required
T34.explanation: For instance a register may count registered enterprises while the statistic needs operating enterprises.

T35.stem: Scanner data from retailers improves price statistics chiefly by providing:
options: Transaction prices and quantities for very many items
T35.explanation: Point-of-sale records give both what was charged and how much sold, allowing weights to update far more frequently.

T35.stem: Mobile network data used for mobility statistics suffers most from:
options: Coverage bias, since it represents subscribers rather than people
T35.explanation: Handset ownership varies by age, income and gender, so the population observed is not the population of interest.

T35.stem: Satellite imagery is most directly useful in official statistics for estimating:
T35.explanation: Remote sensing observes physical land surface, which maps well onto area and land-cover statistics.

T35.stem: Web-scraped price data raise a particular concern about:
options: Stability of the source, since sites change without notice
T35.explanation: The statistical office does not control the source, so the series can break when a website is restructured.

T36.stem: Traditional survey quality measures transfer poorly to found data because there is:
options: No known sampling design or inclusion probability
T36.explanation: Design-based inference needs known selection probabilities, which found data do not have.

T36.stem: Selectivity in big data means that:
options: The data are collected too often
The units observed differ systematically from the target population
T36.explanation: Volume does not cure selection bias: a very large but skewed sample is still skewed.

T36.stem: A very large but non-representative dataset compared with a small probability sample is:
options: Potentially more biased, because size does not correct selection
T36.explanation: Size shrinks variance but not bias, and with huge n the bias dominates total error entirely.

T36.stem: Before adopting a new data source for official statistics, the essential first step is to:
options: Document its coverage, definitions and stability against the statistical need
T36.explanation: A documented quality assessment is what allows users and successors to judge fitness for purpose.

options: The reference model of the Earth against which coordinates are measured
The scale of a printed map
The colour scheme of a map
T37.explanation: The same latitude and longitude on different datums can refer to points hundreds of metres apart.

options: Some combination of area, shape, distance or direction
Nothing, if the scale is large
T37.explanation: Flattening a curved surface cannot preserve all properties at once, so the projection is chosen for what must be preserved.

T37.stem: For a map comparing statistical quantities across districts, the projection should preserve:
options: Area, so regions are not visually over- or under-weighted
T37.explanation: An equal-area projection stops large-looking regions from dominating the reader's impression of the data.
Geocoding attaches a location so the record can be mapped, aggregated spatially or linked to area data.

T38.stem: An area frame is preferred to a list frame when:
options: No reliable list of units exists but the territory can be divided completely
T38.explanation: Area frames guarantee coverage by partitioning space, which is why they are used where lists are outdated or absent.

T38.stem: Digital listing on handheld devices during field work mainly reduces:
options: The need for a sampling frame
Transcription errors and the time before data are usable
T38.explanation: Capturing the listing electronically removes a manual copying step and shortens the path to a usable frame.

T38.stem: Administrative boundary changes between survey rounds threaten:
options: Comparability of area-based estimates over time
T38.explanation: When a district splits or merges, its series is not comparable unless the geography is harmonised or a concordance is applied.

T38.stem: Within an area frame, the first-stage sampling unit is typically a:
options: Defined geographic segment such as a village or enumeration block
T38.explanation: Selecting compact geographic segments first keeps field travel manageable before listing households within them.

T39.stem: In a choropleth map, the choice of class intervals:
options: Can substantially change the visual message of the same data
T39.explanation: Equal-interval, quantile and natural-breaks classifications of identical data can produce strikingly different maps.

T39.stem: Choropleth maps should normally show rates rather than counts because:
options: Larger or more populous areas otherwise dominate purely by size
T39.explanation: Mapping raw counts largely reproduces the population distribution rather than the phenomenon of interest.

T39.stem: The modifiable areal unit problem refers to results changing when:
options: The boundaries used to aggregate the data are redrawn
T39.explanation: Both the scale of aggregation and the specific zoning can alter correlations and apparent patterns.

T39.stem: Small area estimation is used when direct survey estimates for an area are:
options: Too imprecise because the local sample is small
T39.explanation: Model-based methods borrow strength from related areas and auxiliary data to produce usable local estimates.

options: The exchange of statistical data and metadata between organisations
T40.explanation: It gives a common structure so data can move between agencies without bespoke translation each time.

T40.stem: In the SDMX model, a dimension is a concept that:
options: Describes the quality of the data
Helps uniquely identify each observation, such as reference area or period
T40.explanation: Dimensions form the key of an observation; attributes carry descriptive information that does not identify it.

T40.stem: The observed number itself is held in SDMX as the:
T40.explanation: Dimensions locate the observation, attributes qualify it, and the measure is the value.

T40.stem: A data flow in SDMX represents:
options: The order of questions in a survey
The revision history of a series
A specific collection of data reported against a defined structure
T40.explanation: The data flow ties a body of reported data to the structure definition that governs it.

options: The dimensions, attributes and measures a dataset must contain
T41.explanation: The DSD is the contract describing how a conforming dataset must be shaped.

options: The permitted values for a coded concept, each with an identifier and label
Free text descriptions of the data
T41.explanation: Restricting a dimension to an agreed code list is what makes datasets from different sources comparable.

T41.stem: Structural metadata must be versioned because:
options: Consumers need to know which definitions a given dataset was built against
T41.explanation: Adding or retiring codes changes meaning, and version identifiers let users interpret older files correctly.

T41.stem: Adding a new code to a published code list should be treated as:
options: A routine edit needing no record
A reason to withdraw the series
A structural change requiring a version update and communication to users
T41.explanation: Downstream systems validate against the code list, so an unannounced addition breaks them silently.

T42.stem: Reference metadata accompanying a dataset describes:
options: The file size and format only
How the data were produced, their concepts and their limitations
T42.explanation: It is what lets a user who was not involved in production judge whether the data suit their purpose.

T42.stem: Publishing statistics through an API rather than only as spreadsheets mainly benefits users by:
options: Allowing automated, repeatable retrieval of exactly the series needed
T42.explanation: Machine access removes manual downloading and re-keying, and keeps downstream products current.

T42.stem: When a published series is revised, good dissemination practice is to:
options: Delete the series and start again
Publish the revision with a documented reason and keep the earlier vintage identifiable
Publish only the new figure without comment
T42.explanation: Users who acted on the earlier figure need to see what changed and why, so revisions are documented and vintages preserved.

T42.stem: Machine-readable dissemination requires that data be:
options: Structured consistently so software can parse them without human interpretation
T42.explanation: Merged header cells and footnotes inside data cells defeat automated parsing, however readable they look to a person.

T43.stem: The first step in turning a policy question into an analysis is to:
options: Define precisely what is to be measured and for which population
T43.explanation: An unclear definition of the concept and population makes every later technical choice arbitrary.

T43.stem: A question such as 'is unemployment rising?' must first be sharpened by specifying:
options: The definition of unemployment, the population and the time frame
T43.explanation: Different definitions and reference periods can point in opposite directions on the same underlying data.

T43.stem: An analyst finds that districts with more health centres have higher reported disease rates. The most likely explanation is:
options: Better detection and reporting where services exist
T43.explanation: Detection bias is a classic confounder: measurement improves where capacity exists, inflating recorded rates.

T43.stem: Keeping findings separate from inference in a report means:
options: Distinguishing what the data show from what the analyst concludes
T43.explanation: Readers must be able to accept the measurements while judging the interpretation for themselves.

T44.stem: A brief for senior officers should open with:
options: The main finding and what it means
T44.explanation: Decision-makers read the top and may read no further, so the conclusion leads and the method supports.

T44.stem: Writing 'employment fell by 2.3 percentage points' rather than 'employment fell by 2.3%' matters because:
options: A change in a percentage is not the same as a percentage change
T44.explanation: A move from 40% to 37.7% is 2.3 percentage points but a 5.75% relative fall; confusing them misstates the size.

T44.stem: In a two-page brief, technical detail on method is best placed:
options: In an annex or footnote, referenced from the main text
T44.explanation: The method must be available for scrutiny without displacing the finding the reader came for.

T44.stem: Using plain language for numbers means:
options: Explaining what a figure implies in concrete terms the reader can act on
T44.explanation: 'One in five households' communicates more to a non-specialist reader than an unexplained proportion.

T45.stem: A margin of error is best explained to a non-technical reader as:
options: The share of respondents who refused
The mistake made by the analyst
A range within which the true value is likely to lie
T45.explanation: Framing it as a plausible range conveys the idea without requiring the reader to know sampling theory.

T45.stem: Limitations of an analysis should be:
options: Placed only in a final annex
Stated clearly near the findings they affect
T45.explanation: A caveat buried far from the number it qualifies will not reach the reader who acts on that number.

T45.stem: When a small survey-based change is within the margin of error, the honest description is:
options: That the data show no clear change
That the indicator has definitely improved
That the change is small but real
T45.explanation: Reporting movement the data cannot support is the most common way statistical briefings mislead.

T45.stem: Challenged on a figure by a senior official, the appropriate response is to:
options: Explain the method and evidence, and correct it if the challenge is right
T45.explanation: Professional credibility rests on transparency about method and willingness to correct genuine error.
